changes.summary: This display delved into the imagination of Edward Allington (1951–2017), one of the leading voices of the 1980s 'New British Sculpture' movement. Alongside artists such as Antony Gormley, Alison Wilding and Anish Kapoor, Allington broke away from the minimalism and formalism of previous decades to investigate questions of collective memory, pop, kitsch, authenticity and the hidden meaning in everyday objects. Allington once described sculpture as 'looking at real things by making real things. It is making poetry with solid objects'. Fascinated by the survival of classical forms in modern life – replicated across media from tea towels to plastic snowglobes – Allington combined humour with deep cultural reflection. Though celebrated as a sculptor, drawing was at the heart of his practice. Working on old ledger paper, he was interested in the contrast provided by these delicate records of daily life, overwritten by the stark volumes of his enigmatic sculptural forms. A much-loved teacher and writer, Allington influenced generations of artists through his role as Professor of Sculpture at the Slade. This newly donated group of drawings offered fresh insight into his career, revealing the wit, curiosity and roving intellect that defined his practice.
